did_you_know.text: Did you know? The chapter opens with a promise that the Lord will restore Judah and Jerusalem—a phrase referring to the restoration of the people’s fortunes and their return to their land.
Did you know? The nations gather in the Valley of Jehoshaphat, where the Lord is portrayed as judging them for scattering Israel, dividing up the land, and harming His inheritance.
Did you know? The nations’ sins are also described as human trafficking: they cast lots for the people and sold a boy for a prostitute and a girl for wine.
Did you know? Tyre, Sidon, and the cities of Philistia are specifically named as those who will be repaid for their actions against Judah.
Did you know? According to the chapter, the people of Judah and Jerusalem were sold to the Greeks in order to remove them far from their land and territory.
Did you know? In an ironic call to war, the nations are summoned to consecrate a war and prepare themselves for a great conflict.
Did you know? The prophet describes a symbolic change of purpose: agricultural tools, such as plowshares and pruning hooks, are turned into weapons.
Did you know? The nations’ wickedness is compared to a ripe harvest and a full winepress; these images indicate that the time has come to reap and tread—that is, to carry out judgment.
Did you know? Although the heavens and earth tremble on the day of the Lord, the Lord is described as a refuge and stronghold for the people of Israel.

Did you know? The vision of the future includes extraordinary abundance: new wine flowing from the mountains, milk from the hills, watercourses in Judah, and a spring flowing from the house of the Lord.
Did you know? Egypt and Edom are portrayed as lands that will become desolate because of the violence and innocent bloodshed committed in Judah.
Did you know? In contrast to the desolation of Egypt and Edom, Judah and Jerusalem are described as dwelling forever, from generation to generation.
